RE: LR #866 An Act to Waive Basic Law Enforcement Training Requirements for Full-time Law Enforcement Officers Who Have Successfully Completed Equivalent Courses in Other Juris dictions
Dear Senator Moore,
I was recently solicited by my colleague, Eastport's Chief of Police, Marc Podschlne, to write a Letter of Support to further favorable consideration of your proposed legislation, LR #866. Regrettably I've other commitments that preclude my appearing in-person on April 7th, so I appreciate this opportunity to lend my support to this critical legislation.
Thank you for your willingness, and that of your legislative colleagues, to recognize this needed change to permit qualified law enforcement officers from other jurisdictions to attain certification here in Maine. As you are well aware, both our urban and rural communities Downeast are finding it increasingly challenging to maintain sufficient operational staffing levels due a variety of factors, with the ensuing challenges posing consequence for both our underserved communities and taxpayers everywhere. Recent cutbacks in call-sharing arrangements amongst agencies and similar actions have only exacerbated these challenges for our regional and local law enforcement agencies, both large and small. Your proposed legislation, wholly cost-neutral, would greatly lessen these circumstances and provide our already stressed agencies much needed assistance in successfully recruiting and onboarding the highly qualified and trained personnel that would consider residency and employment should their professional law credentials be readily transferable and accepted by Maine.
If I may provide any additional advocacy to advance LR #866, please advise; it would be my pleasure to do so. Thank you again for your sponsorship and support of this increasingly necessary legislation.
Very truly yours,
Andrew Sankey

Testimony for LD 1295
I am Brian Schuth, the City Manager in Eastport. I would like to speak in favor of LD1295, with a focus on Section 2.
Section 2, line 24 requires a study that will "focus on reducing unnecessary or burdensome requirements that would prevent a law enforcement officer who has completed an equivalent training course from qualifying for the waiver." I believe such a study is a necessary first step in addressing the scarcity of officers in our corner of the state by expanding the pool of candidates. However, I believe this study's scope must extend to the definition of "equivalent training course" to ensure that definition is driven by practical needs for policing in the state of Maine. Such a definition should be based on reasonable measures that ensure competent policing, rather than enforcing an arbitrary or academic definition of equivalence. The study must take into account what is known about the most significant jurisdictions that might provide officers to the state. The aim must be to clear obstacles placed in the way of their officers becoming Maine officers, and to provide reasonable pathways to waivers for those whose backgrounds may be incomplete.
This is of particular interest to Eastport: we have had eleven police chiefs in thirteen years. When I was hired as Manager last year, my first job was to find the twelfth, and we found an ideal candidate. Even better, I did not have to poach him from another Washington County department. This was because he was coming to us as a retired agent of the Border Patrol.
I spoke to many experienced people about the waiver process: the Washington County Deputy Sheriff, the current City Manager (who is also the past Police Chief) of Augusta, and the then vicechair, now chair, of the Board of Trustees of the Maine Criminal Justice Academy. Every one of them reassured me that I should not be concerned by the waiver process. We hired our Chief.
In October, I was informed by the MCJA that our chief would likely not be approved for a waiver, as the MCJA did not consider Federal basic academy "equivalent" to the Maine academy - and never had. I was not told why they did not consider it equivalent. The MCJA's only remedy was to send our retired Border Patrol chief, with 25 years of experience, to their 18-week "boot camp" academy. In order not to lose this Chief, we have opted to obtain a "green pin" waiver, which limits the chief to 50% time performing law enforcement duties. In a community whose police department consists of only three full time officers, including the Chief, this is not an insignificant restriction.
At no point when I spoke to other experienced law enforcement officers did anyone ever raise a concern that a Border Patrol officer might not be qualified to serve as a Maine officer. In fact, in Washington and Aroostook Counties the Border Patrol regularly provides backup support to local law enforcement. I offer this story as an example of a municipality that has attempted to provide a solution to an immediate crisis in police staffing, and which has been compromised by obstacles in the waiver process. LD1295 cannot assist us in our current situation; but we hope that it will encourage a creative approach bringing more officers to us.

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Criminal Justice and Public
Safety Committee.

My name is Jack Peck, a d I am the Director of the Maine Criminal Justice Academy (MCJA) and I am here
today to oppose ED. 1295 n Act to waive basic law enforcement training requirements for full-time law enforcement of icers who have successfully completed equivalent courses in other jurisdictions.

Maine statute allows the MCJA Board of Trustees (Board) to waive basic training requirements for newly hired
law enforcement officers that have completed an equivalent training program. This bill, if passed, would remove
the Board of Trustees authority to evaluate and use their discretion to grant or deny a waiver to the Basic Law
Enforcement Training Program (BLETP). The new language in L.D. 1295 removes that discretion and authority
by stating the Board of Trustees MUST grant a waiver.

MCJA staff currently reviews each individual waiver request and conducts an in-depth analysis. This process
includes a one-to-one comparison of course curriculum as compared to the State of Maine training to the comparable training program. Staff then makes a recommendation to the Board of Trustees to either grant or deny the waiver. The applicants' out-of-state training must meet the following standards:
I 90% of the BLETP curriculum which equates to 648 hours. 0 75% of the BLETP curriculum and required to take Emergency Vehicle Operations Course (EVOC) and
Crash Reporting. This equates to 540 Hours. Q All applicants are required to complete Maine Crash Report Training.
A current trend has been that out-of-state Academies are unwilling to provide curriculums with goals and
objectives and will only provide a syllabus with the total hours for their program. This creates a situation where a waiver will become dependent on several other variables beyond the syllabus and hours. These include in-service training hours, years of service and higher education.
All of these factors are considered while processing an out-of-state BLETP Waiver. This information is then
submitted to the Board of Trustees to consider if the applicant is suitable for a BLETP Waiver by the MCJA
Training Coordinator.
As evidence of the desire for experienced out-of-state law enforcement candidates to relocate to Maine and
enhanced agency recruitment, we have seen a tremendous increase in applications for a BLETP waiver.
Between 2020 and 2022, the Board reviewed and granted eighty-six out-of-state waiver requests. The Board reviewed and granted fifty such waivers in 2023 and fifty-eight in 2024. The fifty-eight approved waivers this
past year in comparison, would almost be the size of a typical BLETP class.

Marc Podschlne Eastport LD 1295
Good afternoon, I am Eastport Chief of Police Marc Podschlne. All of Maine and especially rural Maine has an epidemic of vacant police officer positions due to a lack of qualified officers. This lack of qualified officers has forced many local police departments to close their doors examples include Washburn, Limestone, Van Buren, and Mexico. The closing of these police departments strains county Sheriff's Departments and Maine State Police with long response times to both emergency and non-emergency calls and in some cases the complaint/call is queued until the following shift or day. This queue of calls increases the workload on officers in understaffed departments, creating additional stress on the responding officer. This bill is designed to alleviate the drought of officers by tapping into a source of well-trained retired federal or out-of-state law enforcement agents or officers living in Maine. I am also hoping this bill will help alleviate the tedious waiver process for hiring full-time seasoned law enforcement professionals from other law enforcement agencies or departments. It's been tough enough finding qualified personnel without having to drag them through a lengthy process or dealing with a denial on a waiver because there isn't a current Maine Criminal Justice Academy "bridge program." While the intent of this bill is to alleviate the lack of qualified police officers in the state of Maine, it does not intend to eliminate the need of recruitment of qualified people throughout Maine to attend the full Maine Criminal Justice Academy. This bill only serves as a supplemental means to address the epidemic of closing police departments due to the lack of qualified personnel. Too often neighboring police departments are stealing officers from one another. Thank you so much for considering this bill. I'm struggling to get my police department up and running due to the lack of qualified officers. Our police department was shut down from January of 2024, until I was hired as Chief on May 6, 2024, and it's been an ongoing struggle to have any police coverage at all. I have a vested interest in this bill because I believe it will help my department immensely. I am also a retired Border Patrol agent, so I have in-depth knowledge of the qualifications they bring to the table and Maine has many retired agents that bring a breadth of knowledge and experience from throughout the United States. Respectfully, Chief Marc Podschlne Eastport, Maine

Good afternoon, Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the
Joint Standing Committee on Criminal Justice and Public Safety, my name is
proudly represent Senate District 6, which includes all of Washington County as wel as
Communities in Eastern Hancock County. I am here today to introduce LD 1295, "An Act to Waive Basic Law Enforcement Training Requirements for Full-time Law Enforcement Oflicers Who Have
Successfully Completed Equivalent Courses in Other Jurisdictions."
As you all know, law enforcement agencies statewide are facing significant challenges in recruiting
new officers. While departments of all sizes are struggling, the impact is especially severe for smaller agencies, as they have fewer resources to compensate for staffing shortages and smaller pools from
which to draw.
Over the last several years, a number of police departments across the state have shuttered their
doors.
0 Last June, Washburn voted to disband their police after they were down to one officer who
covered their town and Ashland. The officer had been doing double duty for four years but could no longer deliver effective service. 0 Also last year, the Mexico Board of Selectmen voted to close the town's police department, which was down to just two officers. This decision was not financially driven but rather a result
of the ongoing recruitment crisis.
0 Before closing their doors in 2021, Van Buren officers were working 48 hours in a row. As one
former officer said, "[people] cannot function like that."
The closing of these Police Departments strains county Sheriffs Departments and Maine State Police with long response times to both emergency and non-emergency calls and in some cases the complaint/ call is queued until the following shift or day. It is nonsensical to put people in such a
dangerous position when there are qualified individuals who are willing and able to do this work.
In December of 2023 I was contacted by a retired border patrol agent who wanted to start working for two police departments in Washington County. These departments desperately needed more officers
and were eager to get another employee to fill in shifts. First he tried to get a job with the Eastport

Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus and distinguished members of the Criminal
Justice and Public Safety Committee, my name is Rebecca Graham, and I am testifying neither for nor
against LD 1295, at the direction of MMA's Legislative Policy Committee (LPC). Our LPC is made up of
individuals from across Maine with municipal officials elected by their peers across Maine's 35 Senate districts representing communities with very different access to available enforcement resources and local
capacity.
The lack of curriculum investment to create bridge programs or new models of police education
remain a barrier and is far from speculative, with real community examples of communities challenged by the lack of resources provided to growing responsive future models of law enforcement education.
However, as drafted, LD 1295 will do little to change the fact that the Maine Criminal Justice Academy
(MCJA) already does review credentials from applicants who have been certified by other entities as it
simply moves the language from "may" to "shall" resulting in little operational change.
What has been a source of frustration is understanding how those evaluations occur, with transparent and clear metrics before a candidate is hired. As the committee has heard, one municipality
found this out after consulting with the MCJA board assured of the waiver program and hiring the
individual only to have the waiver declined because the federal academies have never been comparable and there is no bridge program to assist adding to their existing credentials. Attending an 18 week
residential academy as a new cadet is not an attractive option for a mature retired federal law enforcement
officer.
As the report on MCJA goals identified, updating curriculum to incorporate modem adult
learning principles that require staff time and resources to broaden partnerships. The chronic
underfunding of the programs and permanent staff at MCJA make this task impossible until there is a shift
in the legislative body's understanding of the imbalance between the communal intergovernmental role of the academy, it's reliance on the good will of local government to support the mission and their lack of agency to drive adequate state (legislative) investment to address those needs.
Also included in the report is a finding that "Training coordinators have competing priorities that detract from curriculum development; there is opportunity to incorporate more adult-based learning principles in the classroom."` . TESTIMONY OF SHERIFF KEVIN JOYCE MAINE SHERIFFS ASSOCIATION
LD 1295 - An Act to Waive Basic Law Enforcement Training Requirements for Full-time Law Enforcement Officers Who Have Successfully Completed Equivalent Courses in Other
Jurisdictions
Senator Beebe-Center, Representative Hasenfus, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee of Criminal Justice and Public Safety. My name is Sheriff Kevin Joyce. I am the sheriff of Cumberland County and I am here on behalf of the Maine Sheriffs Association.
Your Maine Sheriffs have taken the majority position of OPPOSITION for LD 1295 An Act to Waive Basic Law Enforcement Training Requirements for Full-time Law Enforcement Officers Who Have Successfully Completed Equivalent Courses in Other Jurisdictions.
While Maine sheriffs understand the logic behind this bill, we have concerns about consistency. Currently, all Maine law enforcement officers have trained at the Maine Criminal Justice Academy. Every municipal officer, state trooper, and county sheriff went through the same grueling process, but more importantly, we learned together. We all start our careers with the same knowledge base and the same standards.
We are concerned about how to determine the accuracy of `equivalent' courses. While we do understand this bill's passage would potentially allow us to fill vacancies that are prevalent in every county in Maine, our steadfast commitment to public safety comes first. One sheriff in our discussion said it best, "We have a set of standards that we live by and passing this bill would eliminate these shared standards and values."
Thank you for your time and consideration. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have.
